The small capacitor prevents ringing when the amplifier’s output is near zero. In some cases it could be omitted depending on the behaviour of the open amplifier used. Figure 5.3 shows the behaviour of this circuit. The input value has been generated by a single integrator yielding a ramp running from −1 to +1. This ramp has also been used for the x-deflection of the oscilloscope, too.

# 5.1.2 Division

The square root circuit shown above can be easily modified to implement a division operation. Figure 5.4 shows the basic setup: With the multiplier connected to the output of the amplifier and to the input variable $y$, the open amplifier will drive its output towards −x/y, so that the output of the multiplier yields −x which cancels the current delivered through the x-input and its associated input resistor to the inverting input of the amplifier.

As noted before, a small capacitor of about 68 pF should be connected between the output of the amplifier and its summing junction to prevent unstable behaviour of the circuit. It should be also noted that this circuit does not perform a four-quadrant division operation.

Some systems feature pre-wired modules to compute common inverse functions such as square roots and divisions. Figure 5.6 shows an Analog Paradigm MDS2 module containing two computing elements that can be switch selected to perform either multiplication, division, or square rooting.
